text: A language model does one thing: given the text so far, it produces a probability for every possible next token. Prompting is the craft of choosing that starting text, so the distribution you get back is the one you want. This lesson covers the fundamentals; the AI Engineer path goes much deeper.

A useful prompt has four parts. A role or context. One clear task. The input data, kept separate from the instructions. And the exact output format you want, whether that's one word, a JSON object, or three bullets. Vague prompts fail because the model has to guess whatever you leave out.

You can also show the model what you mean. A zero-shot prompt gives only an instruction. A few-shot prompt adds a couple of worked examples. Since a prompt is just a string, you can build it in Python with a small function, and end it with the word Label and a colon, so the most likely next token is the label itself.

Temperature controls randomness. The model's raw scores are divided by the temperature before the softmax. At point two, the top token gets about ninety-nine percent of the probability, which is nearly deterministic. At two, even a nonsense token gets four percent. Use low temperature for classification and extraction, higher for brainstorming.

Finally, treat prompts like code. Put them in templates, keep them in version control, and test each change on a small labeled set, exactly as you would evaluate a classifier. Keep instructions separate from user data, because text inside the data can contain instructions of its own.
Next up: where all of this breaks down, in limits, hallucinations, and evaluation.
